units.title: Soft Tissue Injuries
units.summary: Soft Tissue Injury Injury happens in the “soft” tissues of the musculoskeletal system Muscles Tendons Ligaments Types of soft tissue injuries: Acute (immediate) Repetitive strain Acute (immediate) soft tissue injuries Usually results of a single traumatic event / accident Strains: Overstretch / tear a muscle or tendon Sudden / jerky movement Sprains: Overstretch / tear a ligament Sudden / jerky movement • Contusions: A bruise with broken blood • vessels causing discolouration under the skin Forceful impact from a direct blow, fall or collision Repetitive Strain Injuries Causes by repetitive motion / overuse despite low loading Tendonitis: Inflammation & swelling in tendon caused by overuse / repetitive motion Microscopic tears in tendon fibres Chronic muscle strains: Muscle injuries caused by overuse / repetitive motion Soft Tissue Healing Timeline of healing depends on: Individual health status Age Extent of injury Injury tissue type Injury site https://theprehabguys.com/tissue-healing-timelines/

units.title: Ligament Sprain
units.summary: Ligament Sprain • Common injuries • When ligament is over- • stretched or torn due to • excess range of movement Common injury area: Ankle Knee Wrist Ligament Sprain Injury Grading Grade I Structural damage only on microscopic level Slight local tenderness No joint instability Grade II Partial tear of the ligament Visible swelling More tenderness No joint instability -> mild instability Grade III Severe sprain with complete tear Significant swelling Joint instability Lateral Ankle Sprain Ankle joint made up with the tibia, fibular and talus Occurs when the foot rolled inward (ankle inversion + plantarflexion) • (ATFL), Lateral Ankle Sprain most commonly involves the Anterior Talo-Fibular Ligament (ATFL) in the talocrural joint (ankle joint) Lateral Ankle Sprain Most common lower limb • musculoskeletal injuries for people participate in recreational physical activities Most common type of ankle sprains – around 85% of all ankle sprains Cause: Fall Sudden change of ankle • movement Being hit by hard object Wearing shoes do not fit Walking on uneven surface Sport activities h t t p s: / / w w w.y o u t u b e.

units.title: Tendon / Muscle Strain
units.summary: Tendon / Muscle Strain • Common injuries • When tendon / muscle is • over-stretched or torn when • the muscle is activated Damage mostly localized near • muscle-tendon junction Common injury area: Back muscles Hamstrings muscles Calves muscles Groin, esp. adductors Shoulders, esp rotator cuff Muscle Strain Injury Grading Grade I (Mild) Affected limited no. of muscle fibres No decrease in strength, full • active & passive ROM Pain & tenderness delayed to next day • Grade II (Moderate) Nearly half of muscle fibres torn Swelling Minor decrease in strength Acute & significant pain • Grade III (Severe) Complete rupture of muscle Complete loss of muscle function Severe swelling and pain Achilles Tendon Injury Achilles tendon is the strongest • tendon in human body Connecting the calf muscles to • heel bone Calf muscles are major plantarflexors, including • gastrocnemius and soleus Usually traumatic injury during sports event: Sudden forced plantar flexion Violent dorsiflexion in a plantar flexed foot

units.title: Muscle Contusion
units.summary: Muscle Contusion • Common injuries but overall • prevalence is not available due to unreported cases • Direct, blunt blow to muscles, • causing muscle bruise • With blood vessels damage • Common injury area: Quadriceps muscles Calf muscles Shoulder, esp deltoid Upper arm Muscle Contusion Causes: Contact sports, e.g. rugby, football Accidents & falls Impact from equipment Risk factors: People who play contact or extreme sports Male: female = 2:1 Age ≥ 65 (risk of fall) Malnutrition (risk of fall) Bleeding disorders, e.g. Metro Sports Physiotherapy - https://youtu.be/ddyT7XIyeo4 Diagnosis Subjectiveexamination - onset, • pattern, means to relieve Objectiveexamination: • Acute inflammation: • Redness, jointswelling, • warmth& pain • Joint crepitus: clicking / popping • “Locking” / “sticking” during • movement • Range of motion (active, assisted, • passive) • Joint instability with muscle • weakness / buckling Imaging test: X-ray

units.title: Repetitive Strain Injury
units.summary: Repetitive Strain Injury (RSI) Common occupational health problem Gradual onset of • discomfort / pain Affecting muscles, tendons, • ligaments, nerve, bursa, etc. Caused by repeated micro- • trauma over a period of time, without any single trauma: Repetitive movements Sustained postures Forceful movements Stress and undesirable working environment Vicious cycle of Repetitive Strain Injury IVE – HEALTH AND LIFE SCIENCES – Repetitive Strain Micro-trauma Deconditioning to soft tissues Gradual muscle Inflammation weakness Muscle spasm/Joint Soft tissue stiffness pain 19/9/2025 55 All rights reserved Common Examples of RSI Fingers & thumbs Trigger finger Wrist Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Elbow 、 golfer's elbow( Tennis Elbow, Golfer’s Elbow Shoulders Rotator Cuff Tendinitis Neck Tension Neck Syndrome Back Low back pain h t t p s: / / w w w.y o u t u b e.

units.title: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
units.summary: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome What is Carpal Tunnel Syndrome? Compression of median nerve at the wrist as it passes through the carpal tunnel Carpal Tunnel: U-shaped canal consists of carpal bones, with a dense fibrous tissue (Transverse Carpal Ligament) covering on top Median Nerve & Flexor Tendons of hand pass through this tunnel Median Nerve Skin Sensation: Lateral aspect of palm Lateral three digits Lateral half of the 4 th digit Dorsal aspects of the distal halves of these digits Motor innervation: Thenar muscles (movements of thumb) Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Compression on the median nerve at the wrist Signs & Symptoms: Pain, numbness, tingling of first THREE and half fingers Muscles weakness at hand with atrophy at thenar eminence Wrist pain / numbness that disturb sleep Can get worse over time, early diagnosis & treatment is necessary Risk Factors of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Repeated motions at wrist contribute swelling & compression of median nerve Diabetes mellitus (DM) Fluid retention from pregnancy / menopause Autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis Fractures/ trauma to wrist Female / individuals with smaller carpal tunnel Obesity
summary_sentences: Carpal Tunnel Syndrome What is Carpal Tunnel Syndrome?

Compression of median nerve at the wrist as it passes through the carpal tunnel Carpal Tunnel: U-shaped canal consists of carpal bones, with a dense fibrous tissue (Transverse Carpal Ligament) covering on top Median Nerve & Flexor Tendons of hand pass through this tunnel

Median Nerve Skin Sensation: Lateral aspect of palm Lateral three digits Lateral half of the 4 th digit Dorsal aspects of the distal halves of these digits Motor innervation: Thenar muscles (movements of thumb)

Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Compression on the median nerve at the wrist Signs & Symptoms: Pain, numbness, tingling of first THREE and half fingers Muscles weakness at hand with atrophy at thenar eminence Wrist pain / numbness that disturb sleep Can get worse over time, early diagnosis & treatment is necessary

Risk Factors of Carpal Tunnel Syndrome Repeated motions at wrist contribute swelling & compression of median nerve Diabetes mellitus (DM) Fluid retention from pregnancy / menopause Autoimmune conditions such as rheumatoid arthritis Fractures/ trauma to wrist Female / individuals with smaller carpal tunnel Obesity

units.title: Trigger Finger
units.summary: Trigger Finger Inflammation narrows the space within the sheath that surrounds the tendon • in the affected finger Affects ONE/ MORE of tendons at fingers, difficult to bend affected finger or thumb Common Signs & Symptoms of Trigger finger Finger stiffness, particularly in the morning A popping / clicking sensation when moving Tenderness / a bump (nodule) in the palm at the base of affected finger Finger catching / locking in a bent position, fail to straighten, that suddenly • pops straight • +/- acute inflammation - redness, swelling, increase local temperature, pain Risk factors of trigger fingers Repeated gripping Health conditions-diabetes /rheumatoid arthritis Carpal tunnel syndrome surgery Gender-female more common Management of trigger finger Physiotherapy Management Stretching Exercises: Finger stretches to improve flexibility and reduce stiffness. Manual Therapy: Techniques to mobilize the affected finger and reduce tension around the tendons.

Risk factors of trigger fingers Repeated gripping Health conditions-diabetes /rheumatoid arthritis Carpal tunnel syndrome surgery Gender-female more common

units.title: Tennis elbow / Lateral epicondylitis
units.summary: Tennis elbow / Lateral epicondylitis a painful condition of the elbow caused by overuse may result in playing tennis or other racquet sports an inflammation of the tendon that join the forearm muscles on the outside of the elbow (extensors origin) Management of Tennis Elbow Physiotherapy Management Stretching Exercises: Stretches for the forearm extensors to improve flexibility. Strengthening Exercises: Strengthening • exercises for the forearm and wrist muscles • once pain subsides. Manual Therapy: Techniques to reduce muscle tension and improve blood circulation. Ice Therapy: Application of ice to reduce inflammation and pain.
summary_sentences: Tennis elbow / Lateral epicondylitis a painful condition of the elbow caused by overuse may result in playing tennis or other racquet sports an inflammation of the tendon that join the forearm muscles on the outside of the elbow (extensors origin)
Management of Tennis Elbow Physiotherapy Management Stretching Exercises: Stretches for the forearm extensors to improve flexibility.
Strengthening Exercises: Strengthening • exercises for the forearm and wrist muscles • once pain subsides.

Ice Therapy: Application of ice to reduce inflammation and pain.

units.title: Plantar Fasciitis
units.summary: Plantar Fasciitis strong band of tissue- plantar fascia (at bottom of foot) becomes irritated & • inflamed. Fascia for absorb high stress & strains • Causes Too much stress & strains result in heel pain & stiffness at fascia Risk factor of Plantar Fasciitis • Tightness at calf muscles • Obesity • Very high foot arch • Repetitive impact activities (running/sports) New/ increased activity Signs & Symptoms of Plantar Fasciitis Pain at the bottom of foot near heel Pain with FIRST few steps after get out from bed/ after long period of sit. Usually subside after few • minute of walk Greater pain felt after • exercise +/- Acute inflammation
